On the eve of St. Medard's Day in 1281, moonlight shines brightly on the imperial free city of Nuremberg in the first volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge. Its rays find the street from the strong Marienthurm to the Frauenthor, but entrance to the Ortlieb mansion is barred by a house, a watchtower, and stronger defenses still.

The novel opens in medieval Nuremberg, among merchant mansions, towers, and guarded gates. Ebers grounds the romance in a dated, walled city. Readers get the first volume of a tale of old Germany, where family houses stand like small fortresses.
5544-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
Els wakes late, the sun already high, in this volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, a romance of old Nuremberg. Her father ordered servants not to disturb the young girls, but Eva's place beside her is empty. Eva has already risen, unable to sleep even a few moments, and when the cloister bell rings nuns to prayer, she can stay in bed no longer.

The volume follows two sisters in medieval Nuremberg, where cloister bells, household routine, and young feeling shape the day. Ebers writes old Germany with the same care he gave Egypt. Readers get a gentle, atmospheric stretch of the romance, centered on sisters waking to different mornings.
5545-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
Only one person besides Sir Seitz Siebenburg was not deceived in this volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, a romance of old Nuremberg: the young knight Boemund Altrosen. His genuine love for Cordula, and its unerring instinct, told him she had invented her tale for a purpose that honored her kindness of heart. His calm black eyes rest on the woman he loves with proud delight.

The volume turns on an invented story told kindly, and a lover who sees through it with admiration rather than anger. Ebers writes medieval courtship with subtlety. Readers get a tender stretch of the romance, where love proves itself by understanding.
5546-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
City gates already stand open in this volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, a romance of old Nuremberg. Peasants bring vegetables and farm produce to market. Wains loaded with grain and charcoal rumble along, while herds of cattle and swine, laden donkeys, and farmers' little carts carrying milk and honey cross the dyke, still softened by rain.

The volume opens on market morning in medieval Nuremberg, with trade, animals, and country folk filling the streets. Ebers paints the city's working life before turning to its households. Readers get a bustling, place-rich stretch of the romance, where a market day sets old Germany in motion.
5547-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
The vesper bells have died away, yet Heinz still listens eagerly to the aged Minorite in this volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, a romance of old Nuremberg. The monk relates the story of St. Francis, his break with everything he loved, and the sorrowful start of his life, and could want no more attentive listener. Only the young knight often looks from the window for Biberli, who has not yet returned from the Ortlieb mansion with Katterle.

The volume pairs a saint's story with a household wait, as a runaway maid's absence worries old Martsche. Ebers writes faith and family anxiety side by side. Readers get a reflective stretch of the romance, where a monk's tale mirrors a knight's own choices.
5548-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
The Minorite has gone. Biberli notices with delight that his master did not try to detain him in this volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, a romance of old Nuremberg. The iron now seems hot, and he thinks it worth swinging the hammer. Danger that Heinz may be drawn into the monastery worries him deeply, and he has already ventured several times to oppose the design.

The volume follows a servant's watchful loyalty in medieval Nuremberg, where a young man's future hangs between forge, monastery, and love. Ebers writes old Germany's households with warmth. Readers get a loyal, anxious stretch of the romance, where timing matters like hot iron.
5549-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
A few minutes later, the sisters leave the Town Hall in this volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, a romance of old Nuremberg. Their white Rieses wind so closely about their faces that their features hide completely. Through the thin material they see Herr Vorchtel, leaning on the young burgomaster Hans Nutzel's arm, leave the Council chamber where other honourables still deliberate.

The volume follows veiled sisters watching Nuremberg's councilmen at work, with civic business and private observation in tension. Ebers writes the town's government through women's eyes. Readers get a watchful stretch of the romance, where a veil hides a face but not a judgment.
5550-in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-:
Day follows day, and a week passes with no message reaching Schweinau from Heinz Schorlin or Katterle. This volume of Georg Ebers's In the Fire of the Forge, a romance of old Nuremberg, follows that anxious wait. The magistrate learns that the Siebenburg brothers, with robber knights who joined them, stubbornly defend their castles, making Heinz Schorlin's task difficult. News also comes of a strong mountain position held by the Absbachs.

The volume follows a siege and a waiting household in medieval Germany, where castles, robber knights, and absent messengers shape the suspense. Ebers writes feudal warfare from the home front. Readers get a tense stretch of the romance, where silence from the front is its own bad news.

Course schedule for Management for Equality of Opportunity covers 27 to 29 January 1981, in Room 236 of the Chamber of Commerce Building. The Office of Training and Education's Management School ran it. Instructor and assistant names are replaced by STATINTL marks in this copy. Aims and a timed agenda fill the pages.

By the end, through lectures, readings, films, discussion, and case studies, each supervisor should be able to judge his or her own attitudes, the objectives state. Supervisors should also name leading patterns of discrimination and their effect on supervision. They should grasp the main laws, executive orders, and agency policies, and know the complaint process cold. Sessions work through the agency's own efforts one by one: upward mobility, the Federal Women's Program, and the Hispanic Employment Program. A Black Affairs Program session explains why that program was set up and what it does.

Consultants' report titled Evaluation of PATB and Its Use for Selecting Personnel is dated January 1980. Its assigned tasks were to review evidence for the battery's validity and reliability. The pair also judged its use in selecting staff for professional posts, and its fairness for all applicants, the introduction states.

Two fields were left outside their remit, they note. The intensive psychological assessment procedures were not studied, and nor were other selection tools such as interviews and reviews of school records. Yet they could find no evidence those other tools had ever been validated, they write. Local tests built inside units also turned up, with no sign of validation either. On prediction, a later passage is blunt: across four studies, battery scores gave very little help in forecasting success in foreign language training. Consistent links held only for French and Spanish, it states.

Letter of 12 February 1981 from Roberta Knapp of the CIA History Staff answers Dr. Ivo Omrcanin. He had written to Director William Casey on 4 February 1981 asking about sources for the Second World War period. His interest, from his letter, was a claim in the book A Man Called Intrepid.

That book printed British documents giving Josip Broz Tito a false identity, Omrcanin writes. Its author, William Stevenson, said how this happened was still classified, he notes. The National Archives had told him related material still sat, confidential, at the CIA. Knapp replies that he appears to mean the records of the OSS. A team had spent several years reviewing them for declassification and transfer to the National Archives, she states. The review's target completion date was mid-1982, after which the Archives would process the material for public release. Her information covered only United States government records, she adds.

Eight steps in reply to the Polish Roundtable Agreement are directed in National Security Directive 9, dated May 1989. Routing slips of 9 May 1989 carry the paper to the Director and the Agency offices for Europe. The directive is addressed to the Vice President and the heads of State, Treasury, Defense, and Commerce, among others.

The United States would tell allies it was ready to consider rescheduling Poland's official debt in the Paris Club, and back talks between Poland and the International Monetary Fund. Other steps back private loans, seek trade preference and investment insurance cover for Poland, and set up a business agreement. Training exchanges and private debt-for-equity swaps close the list.

A Fisher diaphragm actuator, Type 657 in sizes 30 to 70 and 87, is covered in an instruction manual dated September 1980, Form 1900. Tables give the core data: yoke boss diameters, pressure limits, travel, and weights by size. Air pressure pushes the stem down, as the opening diagram shows.

A second table lists effective diaphragm area for each size, the valve stem sizes each unit can take, and maximum output thrust. The largest sizes reach thrust figures far above the smallest. Working sections then walk through assembly, including fitting worm retainers, bearings, and the worm shaft with lubricant. The copy sits in Agency files among other Fisher plant equipment manuals.

Venezuela under its incoming president is assessed in a secret intelligence paper dated January 1984, ALA 84-10002. The Office of African and Latin American Analysis prepared it. The work was coordinated with the operations directorate. It rests on information available as of 6 December 1983. The subject is the set of tests facing the new administration.

Key judgments say President Jaime Lusinchi will face grave economic and political tests. He takes office on 2 February 1984. The body follows the opposition as well. The Social Christian Party's heavy election loss puts two decades of cross-party consensus at risk, the paper argues. It also sets up a fight inside that party. The outgoing president and its beaten candidate lead the two sides.

Possible sales of Chinese electronic grade silicon to the Soviet Union are reviewed in a secret memorandum dated 23 May 1984. The China Division chief writes to Donald Anderson, head of the State Department Office of Chinese Affairs. The paper reopens an August 1983 memo to Assistant Secretary Wolfowitz, which is attached.

The earlier memo could not confirm a sale, but reported concern that Chinese single crystal silicon wafers might reach the Soviet Union through third countries. The update holds that Beijing's leaders would likely not approve sales that boost Soviet military power. It warns, though, that export earnings pressure on Chinese firms is strong and central control over many trading bodies is imperfect.

Anti-American incidents in South Korea are assessed in a secret paper dated June 1985, EA 85-10126. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 20 June 1985. Student dissident actions against American facilities open the account.

Those actions aim at President Chun in the end, the paper judges, but they also show a more questioning public mood toward the United States. Many Koreans feel their country is treated unfairly in economic dealings. The body traces ideas on campus: neo-Marxist theories that liken the postwar economic order to colonialism have gained ground among students. Their speeches and pamphlets cast ties with both the United States and Japan as neocolonial.

China's trade in the fourth quarter of 1984 fills a reference aid marked EA CIT 85-002, dated July 1985. A contents list opens the volume. Five figures chart exports and imports by area, sector, and end use, plus trade balances. Numbered tables then give the full detail behind the charts.

The first tables show exports and imports in total, then exports by area and country. Product rows deep in the volume track goods such as synthetic dyes, pigments and varnish, fertilizers, and polymer products across many periods. Like the other volumes in this trade series, the aid is built for officials who need the raw figures rather than a narrative account.

Financing of Japan's great trading companies is traced in a memorandum dated 8 May 1985. The Japan Branch prepared the paper. Its subject is narrow: how the nine largest trading companies fund their business, and how that has changed over a decade.

In 1974 the Ministry of Finance gave banks six years to cut loans to any one trading company to 20 percent of bank capital and reserves. The companies spread their borrowing across many more banks in reply. They also turned to direct finance: convertible Eurobond issues, corporate paper sold in the American market by one firm's subsidiary, and more share issues on the Tokyo exchange. Home corporate paper stays blocked by the ministry.

China's foreign trade is charted in a memorandum dated 31 May 1985, subtitled patterns and prospects. The summary opens with a restart: in late 1983 China resumed buying capital goods abroad after a three-year pause. Foreign purchases then shot up the next year.

Exports also rose as the West recovered, but since September the trade balance has sunk into the red. Beijing has pressed the Bank of China to curb spending by local and provincial firms. Imports are still expected to top 30 billion dollars this year and rise further under the next plan. American sales could pass 4 billion dollars this year. Reserves remain ample and foreign debt small, the paper judges. Wide tables of trade by partner follow.

What Moscow could do to better its ties with Japan is asked in a memorandum dated 17 July 1985, EA M 85-10135. Analysts from East Asian and Soviet offices shared the work. Gorbachev's grip on power, and his move of Foreign Minister Gromyko, open the question.

Since the 1950s Moscow has given Tokyo low priority, viewing Japan as a minor world player fixed in the American camp, the paper reports. That cold approach has mostly annoyed the Japanese who might back new policies. A visit by Shevardnadze to Tokyo could spark return trips and press officials to show results. Any new accords might be more show than substance, the paper notes, yet Moscow could still claim warmer ties.

China's fading support for African insurgent groups is reported in a memorandum dated 16 September 1985. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared the paper, using information available that day. Aid to the three main groups in southern Africa is the subject: SWAPO, the ANC, and the PAC.

Aid that rose in 1983 under Beijing's new independent foreign policy has all but dried up in a year, the summary reports. What remains is some humanitarian aid and words of support in world forums. The paper ties the cut to a wider aid squeeze and to a verdict that the groups are ineffective. Beijing now hopes that nonmilitary backing will cast it as a responsible champion of Third World causes.

Prospects for a bilateral investment treaty between China and the United States are dim, in a memorandum dated 4 November 1985, EAM 85-10188. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared the paper, using information available that day. Talks have run since mid-1983.

The talks now look stalled for good, the summary reports. Beijing fears that settling four big issues would cut into its sovereign rights. The four are treatment of investment, currency transfers, pay for seized property, and arbitration of disputes. Six rounds ended in April 1985 with no seventh set. Beijing does not see a treaty as vital to keeping foreign investment at a sound level, the paper adds.

Mexico's earthquakes and their economic and political fallout fill a secret memorandum dated 31 October 1985. A cover note dated 1 November passes the paper to the Deputy Director for Intelligence. It flags a planned comparison with other Latin American quakes and government replies since 1970.

Two quakes on 19 and 20 September killed between 8,000 and 10,000 people, the paper reports. About 30,000 were injured and over 50,000 left homeless. Damage runs to about 3.5 billion dollars. Less than two percent of Mexico City was destroyed, though some 3,000 buildings were damaged. The disaster will delay economic reform but should not shake the economy for long, the paper judges. Criticism of relief work will grow without sparking major unrest.

Briefing help for a former president's tour is organized in an internal memorandum dated 12 August 1985. The Operations Center, calling for the National Security Council, asked for one-page issue reviews and one-page fact sheets. The material would brief former President Nixon on a tour of the Far East.

Seven stops are listed: China, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, and Burma. Work was due to the East Asian office director by close of business Tuesday. Fact sheets in the file give the hard numbers country by country. Japan's sheet lists a population of 120,691,000 in July 1985, a gross national product of 1,190 billion dollars for 1984, and a trade surplus of 44 billion dollars.

Stansfield Turner thanks an IBM executive for help on computer security in a letter dated 14 June 1979. James Bitonti, a vice president in IBM's Data Systems Division at Poughkeepsie, had met with intelligence community and Defense representatives. The talks covered Defense initiatives in computer security, a staffer reported to Turner.

Turner calls the problem one of great importance for the intelligence community and for national security in general. The computer industry, he argues, can contribute greatly if it moves faster to build more secure operating systems for large general purpose machines. He has asked to be kept informed of developments. A second short Turner letter from March 1977 sits behind it in the file.

Goals and objectives of the Director of Central Intelligence for fiscal year 1977 are set out in a top secret paper, TS 76053. Control markings fill the front pages: no release to foreign nationals or contractors, originator control, and a warning on sensitive sources and methods. The paper is exempt from the general declassification schedule.

The goals come from the Director with advice from the National Foreign Intelligence Board, the text states. They derive from the purpose of the National Foreign Intelligence Program. Specific duties assigned by Executive Order 11905 and by National Security Council directives also feed them. The year's objectives are then derived from the Director's continuing goals.

Education for professional intelligence officers is proposed in a concept paper held in Agency files. The proposal is simple: build a program that gives officers real intellectual growth at the three career thresholds where their duties change. Those points are entry into the service, mid-career, and promotion to supergrade.

At each threshold, duties grow wider and less familiar, the paper argues. New officers must master skills unique to the profession. Mid-career officers must grasp how the parts of the effort fit together, and how to manage larger budgets and people. At supergrade, work spans the Agency or the whole community. How well officers cross these steps shapes their performance and their chances to advance.

Co-locating the Defense Intelligence School with the Naval Postgraduate School is proposed in a concept paper held in Agency files. The school must soon leave its buildings in the Anacostia Annex of the Washington Naval Station. The paper argues that both the Defense Department and the intelligence community would gain from the move.

The merged site would be Monterey, California, where the Defense Language Institute also sits. Students in the attaché program could cut travel by attending both schools in one place, and keep using language facilities during their intelligence schooling. The postgraduate school's degree authority could serve the school's strategic intelligence degree program. The school would keep its own identity as a separate body.

A Director's California trip in August 1977 is documented in a thick file of schedules and letters. A folder sheet at the front notes that sensitive material was removed and relocated to the CIA Declassification Center. The remaining itinerary runs from 10 to 18 August 1977.

Travel begins in San Diego, then moves to Los Angeles on 12 August for a press conference, a VIP reception, and lunch at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel. San Francisco follows, then days at Aptos. The party returns by way of San Jose airport to Dulles on 18 August. Thank-you letters fill the back of the file, including a warm note from the Beverly Wilshire and the Director's own letters of 31 August 1977.

A Puerto Rico trip over the New Year is arranged in a memorandum dated 13 December 1977. The travel window runs from late December into early January. One flight is confirmed: American Airlines Flight 663 leaves Dulles on Thursday 29 December and reaches San Juan after a one hour time change.

The return is the hard part. The preferred flight on 4 January has been sold out for six months, and staff are checking what can be worked out with the airline. Three fallback bookings are held, by way of New York or Miami, or a day later. Fares are listed, and the Agency's practice of covering the step up to first class for security reasons is explained.

Stansfield Turner writes to Vincent Davis at speed in a letter dated 15 February 1977, before his confirmation hearings. He was stunned, he says, when the President pulled the surprise of the Director's appointment on him. About 35 senators wait to meet him that week.

A recommendation from Davis arrived just in time: Turner had told staff there was no time to see the man, then changed his mind with the letter in hand. Reading suggestions are thanked for; he has read one book and is partway through Ray Cline's, while staff pare down the Church Report for him. He promises the dissertation will be sent back before he leaves Naples, where his change of command is set for 2 March.

Members of the Patterson School Board of Advisors are summoned to spring meetings in a memorandum dated 5 March 1980. Vincent Davis writes from the University of Kentucky. A reservations sheet is enclosed and members are told to return it right away, since a firm count is needed.

The usual format holds. An informal buffet dinner at the Davis home opens on Thursday evening, 10 April. Working sessions start Friday morning at the Hilton Inn, then break for a private buffet lunch at Keeneland racecourse above the grandstands, with races in the afternoon. A fall 1979 newsletter is also enclosed. Its reports cover past sessions, including talks on Eastern Europe, Norway, Australia, and a visiting diplomat from India.

Vincent Davis thanks a CIA analyst for a seminar talk in a letter dated 8 October 1979. The recipient heads the Petroleum Supply Analysis Center in the Office of Economic Research. His lead-off presentation opened the RIAC-12 Naval Reserve Intelligence Seminar in Columbus on Saturday 29 September.

Feedback from the audience singled the speaker out as one of the best of the day, Davis reports. His talk gave the most impressive new analytical insights on a truly massive issue, attendees said. Davis apologizes for being a poor host: he and his staff man, Commander Al Roberts, ran the whole program alone and were too busy for a proper goodbye. Biographical pages on speakers fill the back of the file.

A formal invitation to Stansfield Turner is forwarded in an informal memo from Vincent Davis dated 21 December 1978. Davis guesses it may be hard for Turner to plan nine days ahead, let alone nine months. The invitation is genuine, he stresses, and can be answered at Turner's convenience.

Davis expects to be on board at the Agency from 1 to 12 January and is gathering ideas for projects he can take on during those two weeks. He names Dick Lehman among those heard from, all of them good men. He also passes on assurance: many old friends across the nation are cheering for Turner in hard times and a bad press. A formal letter of invitation follows the memo.

Frank C. Carlucci's memo of 9 March 1979 calls a meeting on the CIA Executive Committee. It goes to the deputy directors, the Comptroller, and other senior officers. It cites the Comptroller's 30 January paper on Agency management. That paper also dealt with bringing new life to the EAG. The group is called to the DCI's conference room on Thursday 15 March. There it will discuss an Executive Committee charter. It will weigh the topics the Committee should take up, and how it should work.

Carlucci asks each attendee to bring proposed agenda subjects. They may draw on the Comptroller's list of nineteen, or pick their own. He hopes to agree the first topics and publish a final charter soon after. He notes the group will finish its review of senior applications. That review comes once the applications are complete.

Paramilitary matters, personnel, and the President appear too. So does tactical versus national intelligence. The listed products include answers for the General Accounting Office. The file holds a printed program introducing Turner to an audience. A life story traces his Highland Park upbringing. It covers his Naval Academy graduation in 1946. It covers his Rhodes Scholarship at Oxford, and his sea commands. It notes his promotion to rear admiral in 1970. It notes his service as president of the Naval War College. December 1979 press clippings form a Central Intelligence Agency file with mixed dates. A form notes stock moved to the declassification center in 2002. An Iran page from the year before sits near the front. A Washington Post report is dated 6 December 1978. It tells how the Carter team turned to George Ball. The team sought his advice as the crisis in Iran grew.

Later cuttings reach back to the first SALT pact. Claims say satellite data on Soviet missiles was held back then. The file is a mixed late-year bundle. Iran in turmoil fills part. Arms talks under strain fill more. Old charges on the use of spy facts fill the rest.

Senate oversight gets a full printed report in this Central Intelligence Agency file. The Select Committee on Intelligence issued it on 18 May 1977. Added views from some members come with it. Daniel K Inouye chaired the panel. Barry Goldwater was vice chair. The report sets out the panel's first year of work.

Heads cover the rights of Americans. They cover how spy facts are gathered and judged. Probes and covert action get heads too. So do secrecy and leaks. Added views at the end push back hard. One member faults near silence on the KGB. The volume marks a new era of steady Senate watch.

One year in the top job gets a stock-take in this note. It is dated 27 April 1978 and numbered 24. Turner looks back on his first year as head of the CIA. He marks real use of the agency's end work. The President praised the Daily Brief, he notes. Top staff rated their support high in a fresh survey.

He counts the briefings given to Congress. The count is about 245 for the year. That tops any past year, he says. Open books and papers went out each week too. The average was two a week for the public. The note casts the year as one of wider reach.

Queries from staff on a Europe trip shape this director's note. It is dated 17 November 1977 and numbered 15. One query asks about an official secrets act. No such broad law is in view, Turner replies. Bills in the House would punish staff who leak sources. The papers that print leaks would not be charged.

Other answers touch on how complaints move. A new group was set up to fix them, he notes. The note shows a director clearing up fears in print. Law, leaks and voice at work are the themes. It comes from his second autumn at the head of the agency.

Golden Plate awards will honor the best in many fields, says this Owensboro news report. A Sunday staff writer wrote it for the local press. For one June weekend, the town would host the Academy of Achievement. The dates were June 22 to 24, at the Executive Inn Rivermont.

Guests named in the piece span law and spy work. The attorney general, the Central Intelligence Agency chief and the FBI chief were all due to attend. Some 40 leaders in their fields were expected in all. The report calls them exemplars of excellence chosen for the award. It shows a small river town braced for a weekend of national names.

Report to the President by the commission on CIA activities within the United States fills this file. It is dated June 1975. The President set up the commission to weigh two goods at once. Sound spy work guards the land, he said. Spy work must not harm free institutions or basic freedoms.

Chapter one takes up the rights of persons first. The Bill of Rights stands at its head. Later parts weigh the agency's acts at home against that test. On the choice of a director, the report urges men of stature and independence. Skill in running a large body counts as much as spy craft, it argues.

FBI National Academy marks 40 years in this account from 1975. Its subtitle calls it a tradition of excellence and accomplishment. The tale opens on a Monday morning, July 29, 1935. Washington was hot and humid that day. A young officer walks to the Justice building full of hope.

He was one of 23 police officers in the first class. The piece quotes his own words on the threshold of a worthwhile experiment. A Chinese proverb frames the story: a long journey starts with a first step. The account traces the academy from those modest starts to a renowned school by its 40th year. It sat in Central Intelligence Agency files beside graduation papers.

Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) Houston and California trip fills this itinerary dated 25 January 1978. The trip ran from 31 January to 7 February 1978. Travelers were the director, Mrs Turner and Herb Hetu. Tuesday 31 January opens with a flight from Washington to Houston by Gulfstream, with lunch on board.

Five rooms stood booked at the Houston Oaks Hotel. That evening the party would leave for the Tejas Club. Mrs Turner would dine with wives of Council on Foreign Relations members. Reception and dinner plans fill the sheet. The file is the staff plan for a week of travel, hour by hour, in the director's second winter.

Small group meetings with the Director of Central Intelligence get a working note dated 23 June 1977. The note goes to a staff chief and treats a proposed listing of groups. The listing would set which groups meet with Admiral Turner. Revisions and comments are keyed to the note that went with it.

One change swaps in the operations group of 26 April 1977. For the midcareer group, the course chairman should pick a fair sample of eight. Deputy directors should not shape the pick, the note says. Co-op and intern groups get their own notes. The file shows the care taken to make the director's staff meetings fair and broad.

Executive Order 11905 fills this Federal Register style file dated February 19, 1976. Part III treats the President and United States foreign intelligence activities. President Ford issued the order on February 18, 1976. Its authority rests on the Constitution and the National Security Act of 1947.

A table of contents maps the order's scheme. Purpose and definitions come first. Control and direction of intelligence bodies follow. The order was the first of its kind to set rules for the spy world in public. It barred some acts and set watch over others. A copy in the Director of Central Intelligence's file served as a base text of the rules then in force.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100170006-0:
CIA relationships with academe get a memo dated 11 February 1977. An assistant to the deputy director sends it within the house. Attached is a paper called The CIA in Academia. Professor Gordon B Baldwin of the University of Wisconsin law school wrote it. The paper is an addendum to an inspector general memo of 9 February.

A letter in the file encloses an AAUP conference newsletter as well. That letter went to the agency's executive secretary. It holds a letter the writer thought Turner should see. The file shows the campus question worked as a staff problem in the new director's first weeks: law, norms and ties to scholars all in one pack.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100300001-0:
Letter from Stansfield Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, heads a file built around a Navy game day form. The form comes from the Welcome Aboard Committee. It treats the Navy and Notre Dame game of 1 November 1980. A Splice the Main Brace reception would follow the game. The Stadium Club at Giants Stadium is the place.

Invitations cost $7.50 each on the form. A sender could ask for two, or for more if any were to spare. A check would go to the committee in Summit, New Jersey. The file pairs the director's name with a naval social rite: a game, a reception and a toast in the old sea style.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650011-0:
John F Blake wrote to Turner on 9 March 1978 to forward a study. Blake was Deputy Director for Administration. The study treats a day care center for the agency. He calls it a first class piece of administrative research. He urges Turner to read the memo addressed to Blake himself.

That memo answers the questions Turner raised in December. Turner had put them to the Office of Personnel by memo of 21 December. If Turner approves the operating plan, Blake will take it over and proceed. The file is a deputy's cover note: brisk, proud of the work, and aimed at a decision on child care for staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680009-0:
Summary of the 26 April meeting fills a memo dated 1 May 1977. A group writes to the Deputy Director for Operations. In late April, at the DDO's request, eleven officers were picked by their divisions. They met with him to talk over issues sparked by the Stockwell open letter.

The meeting was long, wide-ranging and free, the memo says. Topics of mutual concern filled it. The group was glad to be asked for its views, collective and personal. It thanked the chief for both invitation and openness. The file records a tense session in the clandestine arm, after a past officer's public letter stirred the Central Intelligence Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300900012-0:
Proposed schedule for the Business Council at Hot Springs, Virginia fills this sheet. The dates are 11 and 12 May 1979. Friday opens with a 0700 departure for the airfield. Breakfast comes en route. The party reaches The Homestead at 0830. The council convenes at 0900 in the Commonwealth Room.

A report on the domestic economy leads, from the chairman of Exxon. Inflation follows, from the chairman of the Federal Reserve. The Secretary of the Treasury adds remarks. A ladies' coffee hour and a tennis tournament run beside the talks. The sheet, kept for the Director of Central Intelligence, is the full plan for a weekend of business chiefs and officials.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301080003-0:
Reagan's plans for intelligence get a press treatment dated 12 July 1980. Jeff Stein wrote the piece, headed Putting the CIA Right. An extraordinary reorganization of United States intelligence is in the works, it says. The trigger would be Ronald Reagan's election as President that November.

A blueprint sits behind the claim, the piece reports. A special intelligence subcommittee of the Republican National Committee drew it in August 1979. Twelve pages long, it drew little detailed press attention until now. Former CIA officials and military men authored it as a group. The file shows the agency reading, in print, the plans a possible new administration held for it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090020-0:
Pace University annual commencement for the class of 1980 fills this program. Four ceremonies are listed on the cover. White Plains sat on Friday, May 30, 1980. New York City sat on Saturday, May 31. Pleasantville and Briarcliff sat on Sunday, June 1. The White Plains School of Law closed on Saturday, June 7.

A table of contents maps the orders of exercises for each campus. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, spoke at the Pleasantville ceremony that year. The program is the printed order for a multi-campus graduation week. Its place in the file is as the keepsake of the days when the spy chief took a college stage in Westchester.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140014-0:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 80-15 logs a panel evening for Tuesday 5 February 1980. A flyer brought the invitation, received on 21 January 1980. The Foreign Policy Association hosted the event. Its theme was Great Decisions and the World in 1980. Members of a panel from The Washington Post would be heard.

Reception would start at 1700, with the presentation after. The Presidential Ballroom of the Capital Hilton Hotel is the place named. The form marks it a social invitation. The file shows the director asked to a set Washington evening: press men on a stage, world affairs as the theme, and a ballroom crowd.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140032-0:
Silvio O Conte heads this memo urging the Director to attend a luncheon. The luncheon would gather Republican members of a House committee. Conte strongly recommends that the Director of Central Intelligence attend at the earliest convenient date. A full list of the Republican membership follows on the page.

Robert H Michel of Illinois stands second on the list. Joseph M McDade, Mark Andrews and Jack Edwards follow. Jack F Kemp of New York appears among the names. Ralph S Regula and Clair W Burgener close the sampled roll. The file is a Congress member's push for face time between the spy chief and the members who held his budget in their hands.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501350001-0:
Press clippings for February 1980 open with a headline of their own. The CIA is becoming a popular editorial subject, the file's head declares. A Charleston Gazette editorial of 25 January 1980 sits near the front. Its title is a plea not to part with something the writer values. Editorials from many towns fill the month.

The spy charter fight drove the comment. Papers weighed how much freedom the agency should regain, and how much watch it should bear. The file gathers that argument in its raw form: small-town and city editorial pages, all treating one question in the winter of 1980, kept in one bundle by the agency itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501440001-0:
November 1980 press clippings fill an Agency file of United States and foreign news pages. An opening essay dated 8 November 1980 asks whether nuclear war had grown thinkable again in Washington. It links that shift to Soviet arms growth, the Afghan invasion, and new United States missile and bomber plans.

Later pages range across Central America, the Middle East, and Soviet links abroad. One long report traces Cuban help for armed groups in Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Honduras. A further report sets out Soviet ties to the Palestine Liberation Organization through Beirut. The file keeps the month's threat focused press writing in one place.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501490006-0:
Frank Snepp, a former Agency analyst, is the guest in a television interview transcript dated 26 February 1978. The program was Firing Line, taped in Washington and hosted by William F. Buckley. Snepp had just published Decent Interval, his book on the fall of Saigon in April 1975.

Talk turns on why he wrote the book and what it left out. Snepp argues that staff and local helpers were left behind when the city fell. He also defends his choice to publish without the clearance he had pledged to seek. The transcript, supplied by Radio TV Reports, keeps the full exchange for the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501520011-0:
Membership lists for the Business Council in 1977 make up a directory held in Agency files. Opening pages name John D. deButts as chairman and list vice chairmen and staff. An executive committee roster follows, with names drawn from large United States firms.

The bulk of the booklet is an A to Z roll of members. Each entry gives a name, a job title, a firm, and a postal address. Marks beside names show active, graduate, or honorary standing. Firms range from Boeing and Coca-Cola to banks, rail lines, and steel makers. The directory fixes who sat on the council in that year and where each could be reached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601680013-0:
Handling of Top Secret material is the subject of a memo to the Director from John F. Blake. Blake, Deputy Director for Administration, replied to a 25 April 1977 request for views. He states that no action is asked and the memo is for the record.

Blake reports that rules for plain Top Secret papers match Executive Order 11652 and its guidance. Codeword material, by contrast, moves faster and with lighter receipt steps by design. He finds no proof that codeword marks are used to dodge stricter Top Secret rules. Attached notes then take up compartmented programs and how many staff hold each kind of access.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601770004-0:
Legal use of the CIA Act of 1949 to aid refugees is weighed in a memo dated 13 July 1977. The memo, marked OGC 77-4483, went to the Director with the act's text attached. Its stated aim is better access to the United States for refugees and dissidents.

The focus falls on lands ruled by harsh regimes that punish free thought. Quoted sections of the act cover secret staffing data and entry for foreign nationals. One part lets the Director, Attorney General, and immigration chief grant entry where safety or the intelligence task requires it. Family members are covered too, within a set yearly cap.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601810009-0:
John F. Blake sends Admiral Turner an enclosed tale in a letter written as head of a former officers' group. Blake signs as President of the Association of Former Intelligence Officers. He states the item did not fit the group's task but caught his eye on a night read.

One marked episode draws his special note in the letter. He reads it as proof that the United States Navy used secret methods long before the Agency existed. The enclosure itself is a naval deck log from the ship Spokane, anchored at Tripoli. Log pages record shore patrol returns, boat work, and daily ship routine in close detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100010001-0:
Economic tables for the Soviet bloc fill a statistical summary dated 25 August 1953. The handbook, numbered CIA/RR IP-341, came from the Office of Research and Reports. Front pages set out terms such as plan, stocks, use, and reserves for the tables.

Marks in the tables carry set meanings explained at the front. Stars flag figures from outside sources not checked by the office. Blank spaces mean no data, and underlining marks figures printed by bloc governments. Rows track output by year for the USSR, China, and the East European states. The tables run from the late 1920s into the early 1950s.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100100001-0:
A fuller set of economic tables is issued in the 1964 handbook, dated June 1964. The volume is research aid A.ERA 64-3 from the Office of Research and Reports. Front text states the aim as sound figures of top reference value on both blocs.

New tables were added and weak ones dropped for this edition, the preface states. A new form joins table and chart on one page for quick use as a visual aid. The contents list groups goods by field, from farm output to chemicals and rubber. One chart sets United States and Soviet acid and fertilizer output side by side for 1955 and 1963.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-00105r000403630001-0:
Lining up the axes of a radar antenna is treated in a Soviet technical article by Engineer Colonel N. Kanonykhin. Kanonykhin holds a candidate degree in technical sciences, the byline states. The piece ran in Military News and deals with bearing error checks.

A test antenna, type PSO-2, is set 70 metres from the radar at 15 to 20 metres high. Pulses caught by the test antenna show by their swing if the axes are off line. The same kit can check sender tone, power drop, and curve steepness, the article states. A corner reflector or metal sheet can serve as a local check target.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100040007-0:
Joint buying of foreign publications is proposed in N.I.A. 5, dated 1 July 1946. The report comes from the Director with full board concurrence. The Librarian of Congress had urged that a wartime joint committee be made lasting, and State backed the idea.

A lasting committee would cut waste and double buying across agencies, the report finds. Its holdings would hold much data needed for national security intelligence work. The Authority should take charge of the matter, the Director concludes. State would run the committee and staff it, with the Librarian of Congress as chairman. Tasks include advice on library growth and checks on orders placed through State channels.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m00666r000301160001-0:
Study terms for Central America aid policy are set in National Security Study Directive Number 2-85. A White House memo dated 9 January 1985 sends the study terms to top officials. The President approved the study, the covering memo states.

United States policy under NSDD-124 holds four aims, the study terms state. The first aim named is support for democracy and free rule in the region. Study sections must sum up growth trends, needs, and blocks to growth for 1985 to 2000. Blocks listed include rebels, weak roads and plant, hard currency strain, loan trouble, and food import bills. Country by country profiles are called for in the same span.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m02313r000100950006-0:
How agencies link to the NSDD-97 Steering Group is set out in a council memo dated 11 July 1983. The memo, marked System II 90863, went to Thomas Cormack at the Agency. It follows a talk between Mr. McMahon and Robert Helm of the council staff.

The National Communications System will serve as the joint forum for the work. The Agency is a chief member of that system, the memo states. The system will shape secure phone and message plans that back NSDD-97. Its plans then go to the Steering Group for approval of final steps and funds. Agencies may join group talks where plans touch their own tasks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m02313r000703900002-0:
Release of Presidential Directive 3 is announced in a council memo dated 4 December 1980. Christine Dodson, Staff Secretary, signs the memo to a wide list of officials. Directive 3 is dated 11 February 1977 and runs one page, the memo states.

Council staff judged that the directive may be cleared in full and released. Holders are told to change their records as needed to match. A second paper dated 14 February 1977 lists old decision memos and their fate. That list marks which memos a new directive has ended and which still stand. Items run from the 1969 council system memos to a 1976 underground test program memo.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10t01930r000200140003-0:
Briefings on spy plane film for the National Archives are sought in a memo dated 10 July 1984. The Director of Information Services wrote to the NPIC chief and the COMIREX chairman. Memo number 84-329 asks them to set up briefings for Ray Tagge.

Film from overhead photo programs forms one of the largest holdings at the Records Center. A 1976 archives review left the worth of the master negative files open. Tagge must judge the set so a call can be made on keeping it for good or not. If the film is judged lasting, storage strain at the Center grows sharp. A routing note sets briefings in July 1984 as the first step.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100080006-0:
Short-wave broadcasts to foreign lands are the subject of a 1941 file from the Coordinator of Information. Opening pages list committee assignments made in January and in a memo that adds to a December note. Names on the lists include Poynter, Warburg, Phillips, Taylor, and Langer.

Planning work is split between secret intelligence and special operations staff, the lists show. Later pages take up the Federal Communications Commission and the use of licensed stations. A shortage of good language and news staff for foreign broadcasts is named as a core fault. Draft letters from the New York office at 270 Madison Avenue seek wire service access for the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100210001-0:
Letters reaching Colonel Donovan in 1941 make up a file catalogued for notes on transport in Southwest Asia and job leads. One urgent plea begs quick action to save a man in France, with a cable from Marseilles quoted. Names in that plea are hard to read in the scan held here.

A letter dated 16 October 1941 from Lewis Galantiere in New York puzzles over a Donovan note of 5 September. Galantiere had offered his services after the President's order set up the new office. A second letter dated 15 October 1942 comes from the Committee for Pan-American Mercy. Its writer urges a plan to match British intelligence teamwork, as once reported to the Navy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100070002-0:
Planning for Project AQUATONE is indexed in a Top Secret volume marked TS 142636. Annex heads list political and cover plans, administration, security, logistics, and medical support. Further annexes cover communications, weather, and intelligence work for the project.

Opening text states the core gap the project must fill. The United States lacks firm knowledge of Soviet war capacity, it argues. Aerial photography is called the most powerful single tool for gaining that knowledge. Flight with current planes is judged too risky, since spotting and loss are both likely. Staff tables then list photo, radar, and signals posts by grade and service for the field unit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100130005-0:
Annex A of Operations Plan 40-57, dated 31 July 1957, sets a 30-day U-2 deployment. The plan comes from the Weather Reconnaissance Squadron Provisional 3rd, Fleet Post Office San Francisco. Control number 160627 marks the annex as a Top Secret copy.

On an execute order, staff and gear move to a named advance base for about 30 days. One U-2 then deploys from Atsugi Naval Air Station once the task force is set. Ferry flight plans must shun USSR and Chinese radar nets, the plan states. Landing fuel reserve must be at least 100 gallons, with takeoff fuel at 1,335 gallons. Kit lists fill later pages, from sextant parts to tape recorders and radio sets.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100390115-0:
Fresh studies for a new System X are questioned in a memo dated 24 September 1963. The memo goes to the Deputy Director (Science and Technology) and withholds support from a 16 September paper. That paper urged an airborne electronic collection program, the reference states.

OSA once backed System X for the U-2 and funded early work by Singer and Lockheed. The gear was meant to fit other planes too, such as the RB-57F. Air Force Phase Three work should be tried and judged first, the memo argues. Spending 150,000 dollars now on gear the Agency may never fly is called unwise. U-2 numbers are already short in the national stock, it adds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100430002-0:
How AQUATONE should be run is sketched in a memorandum for the record dated 8 March 1955. Overseas flights will not start before February or March 1956, the paper states. Key staff must be picked early, while planes are bought and pilots trained.

Two things will end the flights in time, the paper assumes. Enemy counter moves may make flight too risky, or politics may force a halt. Flights should thus start only once a strong force of planes and pilots stands ready. Headquarters would hold three sections: operations, materiel, and administration. Operations would plan jointly with the Air Force Special Activities Group staff, the paper states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300060010-0:
Operations orders for IDEALIST flights are framed by a checklist dated 17 January 1961. On word of a coming operation, branch and section chiefs meet at once, it states. A concept of operations and a two copy briefing book for the DDP follow.

Orders use the standard five paragraph form, bent to this unit's needs. Each order gets a number by calendar year once ready to publish. One codeword marks the order, with a two word open nickname beside it. Cover stories are spelled out for each phase, from ferry flight to staging base. Rules cover aircraft lost in friendly or hostile ground, and who may speak to the press.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300090107-0:
Test work is ranked in staff meeting minutes dated 27 January 1959, filed as CHAL-0549. Mr. Bissell and Col. Burke head the list of those present. A switch of aircraft 378 and a sister ship is under way for engine trials.

The J75 engine test holds first place, Bissell ruled at the meeting. Noise suppression work follows, then autopilot and fuel system fixes. Cost growth on lesser tests must be watched hard, he warned. Publicity for a television event drew sharp talk in the same session. Low key notice would be enough if any word went out, Bissell stated.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300090125-0:
A late primary mission drives staff meeting minutes dated 14 October 1958, CHAL-0350. The main flight had still not been flown when the group met. One interim mission had flown with apparent success, the minutes state.

If the last window of 23 to 25 October nears with no flight, a System IV mission may go instead. Bissell gave that word at the meeting, the minutes record. Contractor bonuses in war were checked and found to be no bar to keeping staff. Contract terms place such staff under military law in war, it was noted. Zoom climb tests at Eglin Air Force Base are also weighed for security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150047-0:
Getting TACKLE airborne leads a commander's report dated 7 February 1962, IDEA-0659. The first mission's launch lit up both sides of the unit, the commander writes. Later missions were then called off, to wide disappointment on site.

Film return by C-130 can meet a tight air schedule, the report argues. Saturday runs would still need a commercial carrier for prompt delivery. Local weather and intelligence support posts were cut to fit the cover story. Engine flame-outs on climbs through the Badlands fill the maintenance pages. A lower power setting was made standard for that climb after test flights.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150056-0:
A senior inspection visit leads a commander's report dated 1 December 1961. The visitor watched a clean takeoff and landing on 9 November, the report states. He greeted local staff and toured the shops for about thirty minutes.

A joint banquet at the hostel on 14 November is named the month's key social event. The writer took command of the detachment on 15 November, the report records. Pilot skill is judged at its highest peak to date in its pages. Housing and work areas are now fully livable, with morale called excellent. Minor faults logged run from sump tank lights to a burnt trim resistor.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150092-0:
Southeast Asia coverage by IDEALIST is planned in a memo dated 11 December 1960, IDEA 0103. Ten sorties in thirty days form the planning base, the memo states. Four ways to stage the flights are set out and weighed.

One staging base crew of about 34 men serves two aircraft, it estimates. Gear near 30,000 pounds must move with them, film and spares included. Fuel near 25,000 gallons must sit ready at the staging base. A C-124 and a C-130 would haul the party and its kit. Detachment G staging in is judged the best of the four paths.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400060028-0:
Terms of reference, filed as Attachment I, set up an Aircraft Operations Center linking the National Reconnaissance Office and the Joint Chiefs. Its stated problem is to define organisation, functions, work flow, and coordination, so the reach of many commands can serve one focal point. The aim is that all needed missions are flown with the greatest possible dispatch.

A normal split of work is drawn. The Joint Chiefs take peripheral, corridor, and special flights, plus overflight missions in active hostilities using military aircraft. The NRO takes overflights over denied areas in normal times and missions needing sensitive third party arrangements. The Special Group keeps review and approval of peacetime peripheral and overflight operations, and mission planning answers to needs cleared by named authorities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400080026-0:
Memorandum to the Deputy Director for Research weighs Air Force against Agency operation of Project OXCART. It quotes the basic document of 14 October 1960, signed by Mr Dulles and General Thomas D. White, which kept operational control of OXCART with the Agency. The quoted clauses put research, planning, and direction of the final phase at Project Headquarters. Mission execution is decided jointly by CIA and the Air Force.

Argument draws on nearly seven years of Project IDEALIST, the joint U-2 operation. The writer finds the choice at once hard and simple. It is hard in sorting the salient lessons of that project. It is simple in that CIA used no magic formula in making the joint arrangement work. Later pages test how far that record should bind the OXCART decision.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400380195-0:
Memorandum SAPC 15135, dated 26 April 1957 and sent to the Project Director, reports an early study of weight reduction for the U-2. The aim was more altitude: every installed item was weighed in the mind against the aircraft's main work of visual photography with the A-2, B, or C camera fits. Items are listed one by one, each with the saving its removal or lightening would give.

Landing lights might go for ten pounds, at some cost to safety, and a drag chute judged unreliable for thirty. The drift sight, at forty pounds, is called an outright necessity for photography and navigation. A tracker camera worth fifty-five pounds is defended for the flight record it gives. Radios, a generator, a sextant, and electronic gear are each weighed with the same plain trade of pounds against use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400400002-0:
Tab I summary of the OXCART program, numbered 2499-67, opens with the end: a decision of 29 December 1966 to terminate the program on 31 December 1967. An orderly phase-down plan, SCOPE COTTON, was put into effect in the spring of 1967. Because spares and engine overhaul carry long lead times, the summary warns that any change to the phase-down must come well ahead of the final date.

The development record follows. Since the A-12 reached full operational capability in late 1965, the fleet stands at nine aircraft, six of them operational. As of 30 June 1967, 2,470 flights had been completed for 4,013 hours, with 757 flights at or above Mach 3. Top figures given are Mach 3.29 and 90,000 feet, and the J58 engine's reliability after climb is put at over ninety-nine per cent.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500060009-0:
Memorandum on a carrier training exercise with USS Kitty Hawk, code named WHALE TALE in unclassified use, reports a visit to Lockheed and to the ship at North Island. Much of the scan after the first pages is badly garbled, but the opening sets out the plan in workable detail. The aircraft was to be positioned at North Island for deck work, with the exercise itself set for a morning in August.

Senior naval backing is recorded: the admiral holding cognizance over the First Fleet and Kitty Hawk was cooperative and undertook to brief the fleet commander. Clearance through the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations is also noted as already explored. The paper was written to aid planning and execution of the activity, and its first part lists information gathered on the visit for that end.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120020-0:
Proposal document 8903-68, dated 20 March 1968, sets out a concept for a photographic film processing system built around near-dry working. It opens on the standing problem: aerial film, originals and duplicates alike, is still handled in wet equipment little changed in concept over the years. Such plant needs mixed chemicals, skilled staff, and large amounts of water and power, and duplicate work adds slow steps of its own.

Contents run from general argument through early specifications, a technical proposal, and the sensitometric character of the product, to an employment concept and a development plan. An Air Force Systems Command technical objective, 93407, is attached as Tab A. The pitch stresses a transportable system giving top quality in a fraction of present time, with shipboard Navy use named as a natural fit where fresh water is scarce.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500400001-0:
Memorandum to the Comptroller of the National Reconnaissance Office deals with buying a second apochromatic lens for the experimental Delta III camera. References run from October to December 1972, and a cost meeting at OSA on 30 January 1973 is reported. The first lens cost 309,000 dollars for design and manufacture, without flight test.

Building a copy from the spare glass blanks would cost about 207,000 dollars, the memo states, while a fuller modification path costs more. It proposes Itek engineering help, acceptance review of the imagery by NPIC, and a fixed price incentive contract, with talks set for 14 February 1973. Funding would come from a photo materials account, since no U-2 funds were free.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600030001-0:
Large bound file of detachment notices and regulations opens with Notice No. 1 on an intra-unit VHF radio network, citing a reference notice dated 6 November 1969. Call signs with identifying suffixes are ordered for use on the net at once. A later notice, No. 3 dated 3 May 1972, covers Dempster Dumpster service and asks staff to crush boxes and avoid overfilling.

Beyond those notices the file gathers standing rules for the same unit. One regulation, dated 22 October 1969, sets how cargo is staged, loaded, and off-loaded for deployments and ferry flights, stressing constant readiness to move aircraft assets at short notice. Indexes and later pages extend the collection across supply, operations, and crew duties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040127-0:
Second copy in the file of Detachment H SOP H-45-11, dated 10 August 1970, on mission generation schedules. Its text matches the other copy: a set timetable for Materiel sections preparing the U-2R for operational, training, or check flights. Maintenance, avionics, and special equipment chiefs are charged with keeping the schedule on all missions.

Alert notice normally comes at least a day before takeoff, and the Director of Materiel passes on the aircraft, time, gear, and fuel load. For weekend or holiday alerts, the main aircraft is named before close of business on the prior work day. Timed tables at the end run from first shop work through engine start and takeoff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050027-0:
Briefing and debriefing practice for the 1130th Aerospace Technical Development and Training Group is set in ATTG Reg 60-8, dated 12 April 1971. It supersedes a version from 22 October 1969. The Group Operations Officer enforces the rules. They cover training and operational flights alike, and name who must attend each kind of meeting held by the group.

General briefings call for the commander, flight planner, weather officer, and mission pilot, with intelligence and security officers added for operational flights. Special briefings use a smaller group. Outlines guide each meeting, from roll call and mission purpose to timing. Set times close the text: a general briefing two hours before takeoff on operational flights, and debriefing thirty minutes after landing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070016-0:
Mode X flight following for A-12 pilots is set out in standing operating procedure 50-3055-24, dated 30 March 1965. It covers flights from a redacted base on routes filed in advance with NORAD senior controllers. Pilots who have not been briefed on these steps will not be scheduled for such flights, the text states at the start.

Notice of a mission goes from the Area Command Post to the NORAD senior controller at least twelve hours before departure. Ground stations along the route watch for the aircraft's Mode X signal. A station that cannot receive it warns the pilot and the next station, which takes over. Any drift from route is reported at once, and pilots must guard security when asking for vectors home.

Memorandum dated 12 May 1969, from the Deputy for Operations, OSA, lists planned Operations Division activities from 15 May to 31 December 1969 for the Director of Special Activities. Memorandum 2559-67, dated 17 August 1967, then gives a TAGBOARD summary for the same deputy director. It starts with the Land Panel recommendation for a high altitude reconnaissance program, optics work by Dr. James Baker, and the Lockheed profile. Approval chapters follow: acceptance of the recommendation by the defense department and air force, presidential approval, and a joint CIA and air force program with covert funding.

Later chapters cover budgeting, development and procurement of airframe, engine, and photographic and electronic systems, communications, and security and cover. Test program chapters run from site selection through first flight. A short narrative bound after the outline recalls early resistance to history writing, and predicts many papers in final form by 30 June 1968.

Set of history prospectuses for the Office of Research and Reports lays out proposed papers on that office and its work. The lead paper, on ORR from 1953 to 1965, would stress the twelve year administration of its proposed author, Otto E. Guthe. It would cover mission, organization, and staff, plus programs that grew into separate offices, and the office's role in economic and military-economic intelligence.

Other prospectuses in the file cover the Economic Intelligence Committee from 1951 to 1967, tracing its subcommittees and its part in judging trade controls against China and a possible China blockade. A further paper would survey ORR estimates of Soviet manpower and spending, with sections on methods, expenditure in rubles and dollars, and the validity of past estimates.

Its table of contents divides the manual into general reports and other sections, with a record of interim changes at the front. The manual fixes how OXCART reports are written, timed, and addressed, so that headquarters, detachments, and supporting units use one set of forms and message formats.

Sample messages show the shape of mission notices: mission number, title, approved, delayed, or cancelled status, and special instructions. A delayed takeoff sample authorizes fifteen minutes of delay and a spare launch on second window timing. Closing pages carry mission tables by aircraft number, with dates, faults such as a failed ARC-50 set, and air aborts, plus a distribution list across agency and air force units.

Public Law 152, 81st Congress, is the full printed text of the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. Its stated aim is to simplify the buying, use, and disposal of government property and to reorganize certain agencies. Title I creates the General Services Administration. It transfers to it the affairs of the Bureau of Federal Supply and the Federal Works Agency, the National Archives for records management, and the winding up of the War Assets Administration.

Title II covers property management: buying, warehousing, use of excess property, and disposal of surplus. Administration rules follow, letting the Administrator perform a function himself, assign it within his administration, or designate another agency to perform it, with that agency's consent or on the President's direction. The act took effect 1 July 1949 and was approved 30 June 1949.

Memorandum dated 14 March 1949, to the chiefs of the ORE groups and regional branches, takes up production requirements. Under ORE Operating Procedure No. 29 of 28 February 1949, the Plans and Policy Staff was charged with coordinating how national requirements are formed. Past efforts by nearly every ORE part met only limited success, the memo states. ORE gained a sound idea of what should be produced, but could never be sure its judgments weighed rightly against the needs of top policy and planning agencies.

A production requirement is then defined. It is a statement of need for a set purpose, stated in definite rather than general terms. It may call for one estimate on a single topic, or several estimates on varied aspects of a problem. Needs from producers and users alike will be merged into a single list for board approval, signed by Assistant Director Ludwell L. Montague.

Summary minutes record an informal meeting on the training of area specialists, held 22 March 1951 at the Foreign Service Institute. Frank S. Hopkins chaired. Those present came from State, CIA, the Navy, the Air Force Institute of Technology, the Office of Education, the Bureau of the Budget, and the two sponsoring councils. Matthew Baird was among the CIA names. Discussion followed an agenda handed out at the start.

Keeping area center faculties intact led the business. A government wide pledge not to recruit faculty away looked hard to get. No general promise could be had that reserve officers on center staffs would not be called to duty. Funding talk turned to Congress and to the Ford Foundation. An interim grant was suggested, so centers could plan for larger enrollments. A Baird memorandum bound at the end assigns follow up action.

Proposal paper, A Project for Training Area Specialists, opens with the national need. The United States urgently lacks specialists who know the languages and peoples of major world areas, and can work on their economic, political, or social problems. State, the Agency, Defense, and other offices all need such staff. University area centers could more than double their training capacity if enlarged and used harder, the paper states.

The danger is delay. Agencies are drawing off the very staffs who must train the next group, and those staffs are too few already. The proposal asks federal funds to train a first body of specialists, marked for their end user agency before training starts. A letter from Robert L. Clark of the Manpower Office is bound at the end.

Memorandum dated 12 March 1951, to Dr. Arthur S. Flemming, presses the shortage of language and area specialists. Scientists and engineers have drawn wide attention in the defense program, the writer notes, with studies and training plans under way. No like care has gone to staff with other kinds of knowledge, needed for the conflict of ideas and non-military action that also bear on national security, the memo argues.

The shortage is sharpest for Asia. It is practically impossible to find Americans with thorough knowledge of the Korean language and people, and the case is worse elsewhere in Asia, the text states. Needs are pressing and growing: specialists must serve as policy advisors, administrators, technicians, and observers. The writer, Robert L. Clark, Director of the Manpower Office, asks to discuss steps, noting a lack of overall leadership on the problem.

An instructor's functions are listed first: running the enterprise, presenting information and ideas, and developing skills. Presentation should vary on purpose. Variety cuts monotony and fatigue, gives repetition without mere duplication, and meets the fact that people respond to different methods in different degrees.

Method choice must rest on what works for a set purpose in a set place, not on habit. Demonstration suits physical operations best. For overseas instructors, much of the need is already inside regular courses, since all staff are potential instructors. Closing rules give each new instructor a portfolio binder of course outlines, held at TR(C) and sent on to his post under security rules.

Case histories have proved their worth in teaching the theory of clandestine operations, the memo states. TRD uses them by study of set cases. A named staff would survey the divisions for cases and supervise their preparation. Each sterilized case would be cleared with its home office, and all limits on its use recorded. In the Fire of the Forge reaches Volume 2 with Georg Ebers deep in old Nuremberg, his romance of knights and merchant families. Ebers gives the morning to Eva Ortlieb, who has not slept at all. She slipped out at dawn to dress in the next room without waking her sister Els, and hurried her maid through every step for once in this volume.

Chapter V explains her haste through the thoughts she carried to her prayer stool. Eva is certain her patron saint led the knight Heinz Schorlin to her, and that he is hers to command. She means to use that power well: to draw him from worldly vanity and make him a fighter for the Church. Sky blue, the Virgin's color, will be her color and his. Piety and first love here wear the same dress.
